title: Present perfect and past simple
objectives: Choose between the present perfect and past simple in clear contexts.
Use already and yet in common contexts.
Form questions with have or did.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: The present perfect and the past simple can both refer to past events, but they present the time differently. Use the present perfect when you connect an event to the present and do not give a finished past time: ‘I have lost my keys’ can mean that I do not have them now. Use the past simple for an event at a finished past time: ‘I lost my keys yesterday’.

You can also use the present perfect to ask about experience up to now: ‘Have you ever visited York?’ Once the conversation moves to a particular visit, use the past simple for its finished time: ‘Yes, I visited York in 2022’. The time expression in 2022 locates that visit in a finished period.

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: Form the present perfect with have or has plus a past participle: ‘She has written an email’. Form the past simple with the past form of the verb in a positive statement: ‘She wrote an email yesterday’. In a past simple question or negative with an ordinary verb, use did or didn't and the base verb: ‘Did she write?’ and ‘She didn't write’.

Expressions such as yesterday, last year, in 2019 and two hours ago refer to finished past time, so they normally go with the past simple in these examples. Ever, never, already and yet often appear with the present perfect. Already commonly appears in positive statements; yet commonly appears in questions and negatives. Usage can vary by context and variety of English.

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: Compare ‘I have read that book’ with ‘I read that book last month’. The first reports an experience without saying when. The second identifies a finished past time. Compare ‘She has already eaten’ with ‘She ate at noon’. The first may explain why she is not hungry now; the second locates the meal at a past time.

The word today can refer to an unfinished period or a finished part of the day. If the day is still in progress, British English often uses the present perfect: ‘I've had two calls today’. If the speaker treats a time as finished, a past simple may be appropriate. Listen to the speaker's meaning rather than memorising a single rule for each word.

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: Do not combine a present perfect experience statement with yesterday in standard English: say ‘I saw her yesterday’, not ‘I have seen her yesterday’. When no finished time is given, either tense may sometimes be possible, but the meaning and surrounding conversation influence the choice.

A present perfect sentence does not always mean an action is still happening. ‘I have finished the report’ describes a completed action with a present result. By contrast, ‘I have worked here for three years’ can describe a situation that continues. Ask whether the sentence concerns a result, experience or continuing situation.
